items.title: The 14-year-old Richard II rode out to meet the rebels at Smithfield
items.claim: On 15 June 1381 the Peasants' Revolt ended at Smithfield. What actually happened?

options.text: The king's army defeated the rebels in open battle
Wat Tyler was killed by William Walworth, mayor of London, and Richard II rode forward and persuaded the crowd he would be their new leader
The rebels stormed the Tower of London and forced Richard to abdicate
John of Gaunt negotiated a settlement that gave rebels permanent rights

items.reveal_title: A teenage king and a dead leader
items.reveal:
Walworth stabbed Tyler during a parley. As Tyler fell, Richard II — aged 14 — rode forward and said 'You shall have no captain but me'. The rebels dispersed.

The charters Richard granted were revoked within weeks. John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered in July. Richard reportedly told a later petition: 'Villeins ye are, and villeins ye shall remain.' The poll tax was nonetheless quietly dropped.
items.why: Successful revolts are rare and brief. The 1381 rising failed in its immediate aims but ended the experiment with poll taxes for 600 years — until 1990.

items.title: Augustus claimed to have 'restored the Republic' in 27 BCE
items.claim: How did Augustus describe his own constitutional position?

options.text: He claimed to have 'restored the Republic' in his Res Gestae (the inscription set up at his mausoleum) — taking the title 'princeps' (first citizen) and refusing the title rex; in reality he held most magisterial powers and military command

items.reveal:
Octavian (Caesar's adopted heir) defeated Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE he made a show of restoring power to the Senate and was given the name Augustus ('revered'). He held tribunician power, imperium (military command) over the key provinces, and the title princeps senatus.

The Res Gestae Divi Augusti — 'The Achievements of the Divine Augustus' — was a long inscription set up at his death (14 CE) listing his deeds. It claims constitutional propriety throughout.

The Republic was, in effect, over. The Principate (early empire) lasted until the crises of the third century. The pretence of republican forms outlasted Augustus by centuries.
items.why: Political systems can hollow out while keeping their old names. Augustus's 'restored Republic' was already an autocracy in everything but name — a useful case in how institutional language can mask transformation.

items.title: The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron enforced the 1807 ban
items.claim: How was the 1807 abolition of the British slave trade enforced?

options.text: By voluntary compliance from British merchants only

The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron (formed 1808, based at Sierra Leone) intercepted slave ships off the African coast; by the 1860s it had captured around 1,600 ships and freed around 150,000 enslaved Africans
By signing treaties with no enforcement mechanism
By immediately ending all transatlantic shipping

items.reveal:
The West Africa Squadron began with two ships and grew to around 25 by mid-century — about a sixth of the Royal Navy. Captures were brought before Vice-Admiralty courts at Freetown; freed Africans were resettled in Sierra Leone or recruited as 'Liberated African' sailors.

The squadron's mortality rate was very high — yellow fever, malaria, and combat. By the 1840s, treaties with Portugal, Spain and others widened the squadron's powers.

The US South continued importing enslaved people illegally until the Civil War, but the Atlantic trade was largely suppressed by the 1860s. Brazil — the last major importer — banned the trade in 1850 and abolished slavery in 1888.
items.why: Abolishing a trade is different from enforcing the ban. Britain's commitment of naval power for over 60 years made 1807 effective — and reframed the slave trade as an international policing problem.
